column3: The Hebrew says one city and explicitly repeats “to him” at the speech; BSB has “a certain city.”
Close to the Hebrew.
The Hebrew explicitly calls the children sons and names a morsel and a bosom; BSB has children, food, and arms.
The Hebrew joins sheep and cattle with “and,” and repeats the lamb and the man who came; BSB uses “or” and “his guest.”
The Hebrew calls the man “a son of death”; BSB renders the image as deserving to die.
Close to the Hebrew.
The Hebrew repeats an explicit “I” with the deliverance.
The Hebrew names a bosom and repeats “like these and like these”; BSB uses arms and “even more.”
The Hebrew says “in My eyes”; BSB has “in His sight.” It calls the LORD’s utterance a word and joins the final killing with “and,” rather than “for.”
The Hebrew explicitly repeats “wife” for what Uriah’s wife becomes; BSB says “your own.”
The Hebrew names the neighbors in the plural and the following actor in the singular; it also retains the image of the sun’s eyes, where BSB uses “broad daylight.”
The Hebrew says before the sun; BSB renders this as broad daylight.
The Hebrew explicitly repeats Nathan and David in their second exchange and includes “also” with the LORD’s removing the sin.
The Hebrew names the LORD’s enemies as the object of contempt; BSB names “the word of the LORD.”
The Hebrew narrates Nathan’s going home as its own main clause.
The Hebrew repeats David and the fasting root. Neither his house nor sackcloth is explicitly named here.
The Hebrew explicitly calls what he did not eat bread.
The Hebrew retains their voice and gives no explicit reflexive object for his doing harm; BSB has listening to “us” and harming “himself.”
The Hebrew repeats David’s name three times; BSB uses “he” in the latter two clauses.
The Hebrew explicitly calls the food bread and narrates requesting it with a verb.
The Hebrew explicitly repeats “the child” at death and names the eaten bread; BSB has “he” and leaves bread implicit.
The Hebrew leaves the speaker unnamed and explicitly repeats “the child” in the hope of living; BSB supplies David and uses “him.”
The Hebrew uses a participle for his going to the child; BSB uses a future “will go.”
The Hebrew makes the naming verb feminine singular; BSB has plural “they named.” It leaves the one loved as “him,” where BSB supplies “the child.”
The Hebrew uses separate sending and naming verbs and says “for the sake of the LORD,” without explicitly repeating that the LORD loved him.
The Hebrew calls what was captured the royal city; BSB has “royal fortress.”
The Hebrew says the city of waters; BSB specifies the city’s water supply.
The Hebrew calls those remaining the people, not troops, and says his name would be called over the city; BSB says it would be named after him.
The Hebrew calls those assembled the people, not troops.
The precious stone is singular in Hebrew; BSB has plural “precious stones.” The crown comes to be on David’s head without an explicit passive placing verb.
